# Introduction

The Reject Inference (RI) problem concerns the challenge of learning from
outcomes that are only observed for accepted applicants, and of using information
from rejected applicants whose outcomes remain unknown. This selective observation
induces acceptance bias and motivates methods for its identification and correction.
Reject Inference has been widely researched for applications in fields like credit
scoring, medical applications or underwriting and rather indirectly from a theoretical
perspective as a missing data problem. Although the research has delivered mixed
results, leading some like @HandHanley1993CanRIWork to question whether RI can even
work, its potential in such high-stakes decision systems keeps driving the search for
this "holy grail".

This work takes in some sense a step backwards in relationship to current literature
and studies RI itself from a fresh perspective. The acceptance bias
occurs because based on (biased) historical data, new acceptance decision are made. This new
accepts become later part of the history on which an institution will base further future
decision on. Therefore, RI constitutes inherently a dynamic problem. Despite that several
authors like @kozdoi_et_al_BE_BASL generate simulation data using such an acceptance loop,
it has not been yet tried to extract information from the dynamic structure of the loop itself.
To do so I follow an intuition: the acceptance bias must be some sort of self-biasing mechanism,
the longer a biased selection mechanism is used, the bias should become worse or become "stable"
in a "non-optimal selection region".

To study this intuition, a rigorous and transparent methodology is unubiquitous.
First, a short literature review is presented, which will highlight the critiques and
methodological shortcomings in the RI literature this dynamic approach might help cover.
Second, and answering to the very valid critique of @ehrhardt2021rejectReview on the
lack of formality in many studies, I use the credit scoring setting to formulate a
precise formulation of the RI problem, using measure theory as a language allowing to
exactly define where randomness comes from and where premeditated decisions of the
institution occur. Third, a simulation framework using the well known two class
Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) setting is presented, which generated the data
used in this research. Fourth, *surprise* is introduced as a way to indirectly
measure the acceptance bias, motivated heuristically from a statistical reasoning.
Sixth, a careful study of both the bias in the logistical regression used for the
acceptance loop and the cross validation (CV) based cut-off selection mechanism is
put in relation to the surprise measurements to evaluate whether the surprise does
deliver an approximation of the bias. Finally, an outlook on the possible applications
of surprise for RI-methods is given as motivation for further research.
